title: Scope: Local vs Global Variables 🌐
description: Control where variables live using `local` – avoid accidental overwrites and side effects.

slides.title: The Global Trap 🪤
slides.content:
## By Default, Everything is Global

If you assign a variable inside a function without `local`, it becomes **global** – visible everywhere in the script (and to other functions).

```bash
my_func() {
  var="inside"
}
my_func
echo $var   # prints "inside"
```
This can lead to unexpected bugs when variable names clash.

slides.title: Accidental Overwrite
slides.content: Watch out: a function can quietly change a global variable.
slides.codeSnippet:
name="Alice"
change_name() {
  name="Bob"
}
echo "Before: $name"
change_name
echo "After: $name"

quizData.question: What will `echo $name` show after calling `change_name`?
quizData.explanation: Because the function changed the global variable `name`, the new value persists outside.

slides.title: The `local` Shield 🛡️
slides.content:
## Keep Variables Inside

Use the `local` keyword to restrict a variable's scope to the function (and any functions it calls).

```bash
my_func() {
  local temp="helper"
  echo $temp
}
my_func
echo $temp   # prints nothing
```
`local` can be combined with assignment: `local count=0`.

slides.title: local in Action
slides.codeSnippet:
calc() {
  local sum=$(( $1 + $2 ))
  echo $sum
}
result=$(calc 3 4)
echo "Result: $result"
echo "sum: $sum"  # empty

quizData.question: Which keyword restricts a variable's scope to the function?
quizData.explanation: `local` creates a variable that exists only inside the function and its descendants.

slides.title: local and Dynamic Scoping 🔗
⚠️ Not like C/Python Scope
slides.content: Bash does not have static/lexical scope. A function can see its caller's `local` variables. Explicit parameters are often safer.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Always declare function‑internal variables with `local`. If you need to return a value globally, consider using `echo` or a dedicated global array.
